candidateRows: An all-loving God who desires relationship with every person would not permit non-resistant nonbelief or the stark geographical distribution of faith.
This establishes the principal hiddenness challenge by deriving expected divine availability from perfect love and supporting it with non-resistant and demographic cases.
After the introductory framing, Joe explains why loving relationship appears to require known presence and why sincere nonbelievers and geographical disparities intensify the objection.
Christianity should acknowledge divine hiddenness as a genuine problem rather than dissolve it, because scripture itself authorizes serious protest over God's felt absence.
This is Glen's first substantive response, reframing the objection as an experience Christianity can ground and voice rather than a difficulty that must be denied.
Joe's argument that an all-loving relational God should not remain hidden from sincere nonbelievers.
Glen accepts the emotional and intellectual force of hiddenness, connects protest to Ecclesiastes and the Psalms, and rejects an overly tidy balancing explanation.
Divine hiddenness also afflicts committed believers and sincere adherents of rival faiths, so resistance cannot adequately explain absent experiences or unresolved revelation.
The move broadens the objection beyond atheistic nonbelief and blocks a simple resistance defense by invoking already committed and apparently receptive religious subjects.
Glen's attempt to locate hiddenness within Christian scripture and treat felt divine absence as compatible with faith.
Joe argues that believers can remain spiritually dry, rival monotheists appear receptive, and sincere Christians disagree on important doctrines without clarifying intervention from God.
Treating every conscious experience as divine presence risks trivializing God because theism distinctively claims that ultimate reality is a personal agent, not merely being itself.
It directly challenges the proposed expansive account of divine encounter and identifies divine personhood, rather than mere immaterial reality, as the harder theistic claim.
Glen's suggestion that conscious, rational, interpersonal existence already constitutes a profound experience of God.
Joe distinguishes methodological naturalism from materialism and argues that openness to nonphysical realities does not establish the much more radical claim of a personal deity.
God can be ubiquitously present yet personally encountered through incarnation, while human moral resistance can diminish awareness of that personal nearness even among believers.
This supplies a distinctively Christian account of divine encounter and answers both the impersonality objection and the claim that believers' spiritual dryness defeats resistance explanations.
Joe's objection that ubiquitous divine experience makes God trivial and fails to establish the personal agency distinctive of theism.
Glen uses the author-and-character analogy to combine omnipresence with personal incarnation, then argues from his own conduct that resistance can impair experienced nearness to God.
The noetic-effects-of-sin defense cannot solve hiddenness generally because moral character and experienced faith correlate too weakly, and defining unbelief itself as sin becomes circular.
This directly tests and substantially limits Glen's resistance explanation using counterexamples, circularity, demographic variation, and the weak relationship between virtue and faith.
Glen's claim that resistance and morally disordered conduct can reduce a person's felt experience of God's nearness.
Joe argues that obvious wrongdoing occurs among believers, unbelief cannot non-circularly explain itself, and populations with less faith do not appear uniquely morally defective.
Geographically concentrated Western atheism may partly reflect culpable intellectual habits and contingent post-Christian cultural developments that distort people's dispositions toward reality.
The argument supplies a culturally mediated response to demographic hiddenness, shifting explanation from uniquely immoral individuals to inherited intellectual and institutional trajectories.
Joe's contention that sin cannot explain why faith is geographically uneven because moral character does not track belief closely enough.
Glen distinguishes individual blame from entrenched patterns of reasoning and presents Western secularization as a contingent historical process capable of shaping religious perception.
Even if cultural history weakens a person's natural awareness of God without personal fault, perfect love should provide a clear revelation when that person becomes responsible for belief.
This grants Glen's cultural diagnosis while arguing that it fails to justify continued silence, thereby preserving the non-resistant hiddenness challenge under the proposed explanation.
Glen's proposal that contingent post-Christian intellectual history can corrupt people's intuitive awareness of God without making each individual uniquely blameworthy.

Joe imagines a culturally disadvantaged but nonculpable person reaching intellectual maturity and argues that a loving God should then intervene clearly enough to permit responsible acceptance or rejection.
The crucified Christ grounds the reality of divine hiddenness and offers a trustworthy God who enters humanity's God-forsaken suffering rather than explaining it from a distance.
This is Glen's principal positive Christian answer to hiddenness, arguing that Christianity uniquely depicts God sharing abandonment and thereby warrants trust despite lacking a full explanation.
Joe's argument that a loving God should directly reveal himself to culturally disadvantaged people once they become responsible for their beliefs.
Glen portrays humanity as entangled in personal and structural evil, identifies the forsaken Christ as divine self-revelation, and offers solidarity and trust rather than a complete solution.

Gratuitous-seeming horrors make evil experientially forceful, yet skeptical theism may be the strongest available response because finite humans cannot expect to comprehend an omniscient creator's reasons.
The move introduces the debate's second major issue, articulates the evidential force of apparently pointless suffering, and identifies epistemic humility as the strongest theistic defense.
Joe invokes children suffering extreme harms to resist abstract treatment of evil, then appeals to Job and the vast cognitive distance between humanity and a possible omniscient creator.
The Christian narrative makes suffering intelligible by identifying Jesus as the divine person who bears creation's cost and judges resurrection worth that cost.
This directly develops the Christian answer to evil by joining human epistemic limits to divine participation in suffering and the prospect of resurrection.
Joe Folley's claim that Job supports accepting our inability to comprehend God's reasons for evil.
After Joe appeals to Job and human finitude, Glen accepts the limits of human calculation but argues that the gospel identifies Jesus as able to make and personally bear that calculation.
Skeptical theism can address evil and hiddenness, but excessive reliance on divine inscrutability undermines arguments from divine goodness and fine-tuning.
It identifies an internal tradeoff in the theistic defense: the inscrutability needed to answer evil may defeat the intelligibility needed for other theistic arguments.
Glen Scrivener's appeal to Job, Christ, and divine comprehension as a response to apparently pointless suffering.
Joe grants the appeal of Job's mystery and the special role assigned to Jesus, then argues that a God made too unfathomable cannot reliably ground goodness or purposive fine-tuning.
Christian theology cannot make God wholly incommunicable because the unity of God and Christ connects divine life directly with embodied human suffering.
The argument answers the inscrutability objection by supplying a specifically Christian limit on skeptical theism and reconnecting God with experienced suffering.
Joe Folley's warning that making God's reasoning too unfathomable damages Christianity's other claims about God.
Glen concedes that the earlier ant analogy risks excessive distance, then argues that Christian claims about God and Christ prevent separating divine reality from earthly suffering.
A personal divine commander may motivate morality better than an impersonal Platonic good, yet grounding motivation in divine power risks reducing morality to coercion.
It grants a major advantage to theistic morality while formulating a dilemma about whether goodness motivates intrinsically or only through God's superior power.
Glen Scrivener's suggestion that a genuine objection to evil requires a moral grounding that naturalism struggles to provide.

Joe argues that theism supplies both normative and practical enforcement absent from impersonal realism, but contends that this advantage becomes morally troubling if obedience ultimately rests on threatened consequences.
The Trinity answers the Euthyphro dilemma by grounding goodness in an eternal, personal community of other-directed love rather than arbitrariness or an external standard.
This supplies the positive Christian account of objective morality, presenting divine love as simultaneously personal, normative, non-arbitrary, and motivational.
Joe Folley's dilemma between an impersonal good that may not motivate and divine commands backed merely by coercive power.
Glen frames the standard dilemma about whether goodness depends on God, then argues that eternal reciprocal love within the Trinity identifies God's life itself with goodness.
Every moral system must bridge description and normativity, although the interpersonal character of theism may make that transition to obligation easier than alternatives do.
It preserves the is-to-ought challenge against theism while conceding that divine interpersonal command may provide a stronger route to practical obligation.
Glen Scrivener's claim that Trinitarian divine love personally grounds goodness and avoids the Euthyphro dilemma.

Joe notes affinities between Christian and Neoplatonic accounts, then argues that identifying something as good does not itself yield obligation, while granting that relation to a divine person narrows the gap.
Naturalism describes blind indifference but cannot account for objective wrongness, whereas Christianity supplies the standard by which suffering can be condemned as genuinely evil.
This directly advances the motion's comparative claim that Christian theism better explains objective moral judgment, especially our condemnation of severe suffering.
Glen shifts the discussion to morality and argues that descriptions of an indifferent universe omit the normative wrongness perceived in suffering, which requires a standard of objective rightness.
Moral anti-realism can make moral judgment inherently motivating by incorporating emotion, avoiding the realist possibility of recognizing goodness without caring about it.
The argument offers a substantive non-theistic alternative in moral explanation by treating motivation as internal to affective moral judgment rather than externally added.
Glen Scrivener's contention that naturalism cannot explain objective wrongness and that Christianity provides the needed moral standard.
Joe considers reflective-agency constructivism but emphasizes the persistent gap between moral propositions and motivation, presenting emotive anti-realism as especially strong on motivating action.
Anti-realism struggles to classify opposing moral attitudes as right or wrong, while theism provides one plausible but not uniquely necessary route to moral realism.
This concession clarifies the principal weakness of the non-realist alternative while resisting the stronger conclusion that only theism can secure moral truth.
Glen Scrivener's objection that emotivism cannot say a person approving murder has made a genuinely wrong moral judgment.

Joe accepts that bare anti-realism cannot adjudicate competing approvals and disapprovals, and suggests that theism can combine realist truth with emotive motivation while remaining one option among others.
Much apparent contemporary moral disagreement is factual, but genuine foundational disagreement becomes clearer across historical periods because moral outlooks reflect shared cultural formation.
The move bears on whether objective morality needs theism by explaining present consensus sociologically while acknowledging deeper historical moral variation.
Glen Scrivener's challenge that anti-realism cannot condemn public approval of murder as objectively mistaken.

Joe grants the attraction of realism and theism but argues that many heated disputes concern descriptive status rather than basic values, before noting that wider historical comparison reveals more genuine divergence.
Religion motivates moral conduct through a narrative framework more effectively than a merely propositional grounding of moral realism.
The claim directly addresses whether religious belief has a distinctive explanatory and motivational advantage in the domain of morality.
After agreeing that sacred descriptions carry prescriptive content, Folley argues that ordinary moral motivation rests on stories and that religion supplies such a narrative structure.
Modern human-rights discourse retains Christian ideas of human dignity while materialist modernity has traded integrated meaning for technological power.
This connects contemporary moral equality to Christian intellectual inheritance and challenges materialism's ability to sustain its inherited moral language.
Scrivener accepts the importance of narrative, links rights and equality to the image of God, and contrasts that inheritance with modernity's mechanistic separation of facts and values.
Using Christianity's historical moral influence apologetically requires prior criteria for distinguishing genuine doctrinal development from corruption.
The objection challenges the inferential force of the Dominion thesis by arguing that hindsight alone cannot identify Christian moral progress rather than corruption.
The earlier claim that Christianity's narrative and inherited concepts explain the development of modern moral equality.

Folley observes that abolition now appears biblically obvious although it was once disputed, then uses other contested developments to demand philosophical and theological standards independent of hindsight.
The image of God and sanctity of life provide a boundary by which some compassionate-sounding changes can be identified as genuinely post-Christian.
The move supplies a concrete proposed boundary for answering the central corruption-versus-development objection to Christianity's moral genealogy.
Folley's demand for advance criteria that distinguish Christian moral flowerings from corruptions.
Scrivener cites Holland's treatment of euthanasia and late-term abortion, arguing that appeals to compassion cease to be Christian when they violate divine-image dignity and life's sanctity.
Scripture, centered on its governing narrative, can stand above institutional Christianity and judge whether historical developments are faithful or corrupt.
This proposes an authority external to historical Christian practice that can evaluate moral changes, directly addressing the principal epistemic challenge raised by Folley.
Folley's argument that Christian genealogy alone has little theological significance and cannot validate a moral development.

Scrivener distinguishes Catholic and Protestant readings of the Dominion story and argues that Protestantism places scripture above the church, while acknowledging the problem of how scripture is interpreted.
A realist account of moral development must explain delayed discovery without retrofitting progress or surrendering the timelessness of moral truth.
The argument exposes a structural tension in the Christian realist explanation of moral progress and demands a predictive method for identifying progress and regression.
Scrivener's proposal that scripture can judge Christian history and separate faithful development from corruption.

Folley argues that eternal truths must somehow be gradually uncovered, warns against fitting standards to whatever history produced, and insists that the flowering metaphor cannot substitute for a usable process.
Biblical moral development has a discernible shape in which God patiently regulates nonideal conditions while Jesus restores creation's intended moral order.
The move gives the Christian model substantive narrative content rather than an abstract metaphor, addressing how fixed ideals can unfold through contingent history.
Folley's challenge that moral realism needs a concrete process for recognizing genuine development and missteps.

Using biblical teaching on divorce, Genesis, Jesus's growth parables, and the contingent Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Scrivener describes patient movement from accommodation toward an enduring ideal.
Ancient Christian truths will yield new moral applications when technological and historical shocks expose problems that existing practice has not resolved.
The claim extends the Christian account of moral progress into future cases and presents the image of God as indispensable for navigating emerging technological pressures.
Folley's concern that a timeless moral truth account must explain whether further moral discoveries remain possible.

Scrivener attributes moral discovery to encounters with contingent shocks, invokes slavery as a precedent, and predicts that artificial intelligence will renew the need for divine-image accounts of humanity.
The cruciform Jesus narrative supplies the governing criterion for judging whether actions taken in Christianity's name represent moral progress or regression.
This is Scrivener's direct answer to the debate's central adjudicative problem: how Christianity can identify moral progress without merely endorsing its own history.
Folley's objection that Christians need a reliable way to identify backward steps committed in Jesus's name.

Scrivener locates authority in scripture's Jesus-centered narrative rather than isolated proof texts or an abstract synthesis, using the forgiving, self-giving crucified Christ as the evaluative pattern.
Embodied participation in the Jesus story will remain a durable source of moral progress despite inevitable historical distortions and wrong turns.
The concluding claim crystallizes the pro side's case that Christianity's enacted narrative can continue generating moral formation and progress through imperfect history.
Folley's observation that emotional formation remains morally important even for people who affirm cognitive moral truths.

Pointing to the church's images, communion, song, embodiment, and exchange of peace, Scrivener argues that enacted Christian narrative nourishes moral progress while conceding future twists and failures.
